Message Passing on the Edge:
Towards Scalable and Expressive GNNs

Pablo Barceló Affiliation: IMC UC, CENIA & IMFD Email: pbarcelo@uc.cl    Fabian Jogl Affiliation: TU Wien Email: fabian.jogl@tuwien.ac.at    Alexander Kozachinskiy Affiliation: CENIA Email: alexander.kozachinskyi@cenia.cl    Matthias Lanzinger Affiliation: TU Wien Email: matthias.lanzinger@tuwien.ac.at    Stefan Neumann Affiliation: TU Wien Email: stefan.neumann@tuwien.ac.at    Cristóbal Rojas Affiliation: IMC UC & CENIA Email: luis.rojas@uc.cl
Abstract

We propose EB-1WL, an edge-based color-refinement test, and a corresponding GNN architecture, EB-GNN. Our architecture is inspired by a classic triangle counting algorithm by Chiba and Nishizeki, and explicitly uses triangles during message passing. We achieve the following results: (1) EB-1WL is significantly more expressive than 1-WL. Further, we provide a complete logical characterization of EB-1WL based on first-order logic, and matching distinguishability results based on homomorphism counting. (2) In an important distinction from previous proposals for more expressive GNN architectures, EB-1WL and EB-GNN require near-linear time and memory on practical graph learning tasks. (3) Empirically, we show that EB-GNN is a highly-efficient general-purpose architecture: It substantially outperforms simple MPNNs, and remains competitive with task-specialized GNNs while being significantly more computationally efficient.

1 Introduction

Graph learning, and in particular message-passing graph neural networks (GNNs), have emerged as a fundamental tool across the sciences (Scarselli et al., 2009; Kipf & Welling, 2017; Wu et al., 2019). A major factor in the wide applicability of GNNs is the robust theoretical framework that grounds their study in principled comparisons between architectures. Core to this framework is the characterization of the expressive power of GNNs in terms of the Weisfeiler–Leman (1WL) test, a central notion in the theoretical study of graph similarity (Morris et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2019). Owing to this connection, alternative, yet equally insightful, characterizations of GNN expressive power have been developed—such as via finite-variable fragments of counting logics (Cai et al., 1992) or homomorphism counts from classes of graphs of bounded treewidth (Dvorák, 2010; Dell et al., 2018).

While these perspectives enrich our understanding of GNN capabilities, they also make clear that 1WL-based GNNs remain limited in important ways. To highlight the necessity for more expressive tests than 1WL, an illustrative limitation of 1WL-based GNNs is their inability to detect small motifs or count triangles (Chen et al., 2020; Arvind et al., 2020; Lanzinger & Barceló, 2024). The higher-order WL hierarchy offers a systematic remedy: properties that elude 1WL are often captured at some higher level, i.e., by kkWL for some k>1k>1. Yet this increase in expressive power comes at a steep computational cost. Even GNNs inspired by 2WL demand quadratic memory and cubic runtime in the number of nodes, rendering them impractical for large graphs (Maron et al., 2019). This creates a central challenge: to bridge the gap between the tractability of 1WL and the expressivity of 2WL. Importantly, progress on this front must rest on strong theoretical foundations—whether refined isomorphism tests, logical characterizations, or homomorphism-count perspectives—so that the precise expressive power of new architectures is rigorously understood.

Recent work on the so-called neighbor-communication 1WL (NC-1WL) test (Liu et al., 2024) moves in this direction, extending 1WL by incorporating edge information within the neighborhood of each node in the graph. NC-1WL is strictly more expressive than 1WL and remains efficient, making it an attractive refinement from a practical standpoint. However, from a theoretical perspective, its study remains incomplete: while NC-1WL has a well-defined placement within the WL hierarchy, it lacks the wealth of alternative characterizations (e.g., logical or homomorphism-count based) that have proven essential in understanding the power and limitations of 1WL and its higher-dimensional variants. Moreover, its computational complexity has not been subjected to a refined analysis, leaving open how well its efficiency scales across graph classes of varying density.

We build on the previous framework but switch the focus from nodes to edges, achieving a clear improvement in expressivity without increasing complexity. This shift yields a more powerful yet elegantly simple architecture, whose theoretical properties follow naturally from its design. Guided by this idea, we introduce the edge-based 1WL test (EB-1WL)—a refinement of 1WL that remains computationally efficient and rigorously grounded. EB-1WL updates edge colors through incidence relations and triangle-induced interactions (see Fig. 1 and Sec. 3), an edge-centric perspective inspired by the classic triangle-counting algorithm of Chiba & Nishizeki (1985). This approach retains much of 2WL’s relational strength while avoiding its combinatorial blowup: each iteration runs in O⁡(α​m)O(\alpha m) time, where mm is the number of edges and α\alpha is the graph’s arboricity.

Since α\alpha is typically small in real-world graphs11 1 In all 39 datasets considered by Eppstein et al. (2013), the arboricity is at most 201 even though their largest graph has 3.7 million nodes and 16.5 million edges. On 32/39 of their datasets, the arboricity is less than 60. We note that Eppstein et al. (2013) report the degeneracy, which is an upper bound on the arboricity. , EB-1WL achieves near-linear performance in practice. We further give three expressiveness results for EB1-WL:

  1. 1.

    EB-1WL strictly extends the expressive power of NC-1WL.

  2. 2.

    On the logical side, it admits a precise characterization in terms of clique-based finite-variable fragments with counting quantifiers.

  3. 3.

    On the homomorphism-count side, we prove a lower bound, showing that EB-1WL is at least as powerful as counting homomorphisms from chordal graphs of treewidth two.

In combination, these results position EB-1WL as a natural generalization of the 1WL test, while still being highly efficient in practice. Its improvement in expressivity over 1WL/NC-1WL is due to a conceptual change in the architecture—not a heuristic variant, but a principled intermediate point in the WL hierarchy.

Building on this foundation, we introduce EB-GNNs, a message-passing architecture that exactly matches the expressive power of EB-1WL. EB-GNNs perform strongly across diverse settings: (1) on synthetic benchmarks, they capture structural patterns far beyond triangle counts and, in some cases, rival higher-order tests; (2) on molecular datasets, they outperform standard baselines and remain competitive with task-specialized GNNs while being significantly more computationally efficient; and (3) on large-scale graphs, they scale effectively and achieve state-of-the-art accuracy. Together, these results establish EB-GNNs as an expressive yet highly efficient general-purpose architecture.

Further related work.

Surprisingly, edge-based GNN architectures are rare in the literature. Most directly, Zhang et al. (2020) propose an architecture based on edge convolution. Additionally, Cai et al. (2022) studied the application of standard message-passing GNNs to the line graph22 2 In the line graph of a graph GG, the edges of GG become vertices that are connected according to their incidences in GG. for link prediction. However, the theoretical properties of these approaches remain unexplored. Moreover, so-called local versions of 2WL assign colors to each pair of vertices while enforcing constraints for node pairs corresponding to edges (Morris et al., 2020). While this refinement is more scalable than plain 2WL, it still requires processing all node pairs. In contrast, our proposed EB-GNNs differ substantially from these methods: rather than adapting classic WL-style message passing to edges, we leverage established algorithmic insights to introduce a fundamentally new type of message passing (cf. Fig 1) that is only possible at the edge level.

2 Preliminaries

Graphs.

We study undirected graphs G=(V,E)G=(V,E), where VV is the set of vertices and E⊆(V2)E\subseteq\binom{V}{2} is the set of edges. We set n=|V|n=|V| and m=|E|m=|E|. We write N⁡(v):={w∣{v,w}∈E}N(v):=\{w\mid\{v,w\}\in E\} for the neighborhood of v∈Vv\in V. For technical simplicity, we assume that graphs do not have isolated nodes.

WL test.

The Weisfeiler–Leman test (WL test) is a family of combinatorial algorithms for distinguishing graphs through iterative refinement of vertex- or tuple-colorings (Weisfeiler & Leman, 1968; Cai et al., 1992). The most widely used variant is the 1WL test, or color refinement. Given a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), this algorithm assigns each vertex v∈Vv\in V a color 𝖼𝗋(ℓ)​(G,v){\sf cr}^{(\ell)}(G,v) at iteration ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0, defined inductively as follows: the initial color is constant, 𝖼𝗋(0)​(G,v):=1{\sf cr}^{(0)}(G,v):=1, and the update rule is

𝖼𝗋(ℓ+1)​(G,v):=(𝖼𝗋(ℓ)​(G,v),{{𝖼𝗋(ℓ)​(G,u)∣u∈N⁡(v)}}).{\sf cr}^{(\ell+1)}(G,v):=\big(\,{\sf cr}^{(\ell)}(G,v),\,\{\!\{{\sf cr}^{(\ell)}(G,u)\mid u\in N(v)\}\!\}\,\big).

At each iteration ℓ\ell, the coloring induces a partition of the vertex set of GG, where the partition at iteration ℓ+1\ell+1 always refines that at iteration ℓ\ell. Once this process stabilizes, we write 𝖼𝗋⁡(G,v){\sf cr}(G,v) for the final color assigned to vertex vv. We define 𝖼𝗋⁡(G){\sf cr}(G) as the multiset {{𝖼𝗋⁡(G,v)∣v∈V}}\{\!\{{\sf cr}(G,v)\mid v\in V\}\!\}, and call two graphs GG and G′G^{\prime} distinguishable by 1WL if 𝖼𝗋⁡(G)≠𝖼𝗋⁡(G′){\sf cr}(G)\neq{\sf cr}(G^{\prime}).

Higher-order versions of the WL test are also widely studied in the literature. Rather than focusing on individual vertices, the kkWL test, for k>1k>1, considers kk-tuples of vertices. Each kk-tuple is assigned a color that reflects the isomorphism type of the subgraph induced by those vertices. At each refinement step, the color of a kk-tuple is updated by considering all possible ways of replacing one of its vertices with another vertex in the graph. For example, when k=2k=2, each ordered pair (u,v)(u,v) refines its color by looking at pairs such as (u,w)(u,w) and (w,v)(w,v) for all possible ww. In this way, the kkWL test captures not only the view of individual vertices, but also the structural relations within patterns of size kk.

Neighbor-communication WL test.

An extension of 1WL that incorporates information about the edges between the neighbors of a node has been proposed recently (Liu et al., 2024). The resulting test, called NC-1WL test, where NC stands for neighbor communication, proceeds similarly to 1WL, but updates the color 𝗇𝖼(ℓ)​(G,v){\sf nc}^{(\ell)}(G,v) of each vertex vv in a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) according to the rule

𝗇𝖼(ℓ+1)​(G,v):=\displaystyle{\sf nc}^{(\ell+1)}(G,v):= (𝗇𝖼(ℓ)​(G,v),{{𝗇𝖼(ℓ)​(G,u)∣u∈N⁡(v)}}CLOSE,\displaystyle\big(\,{\sf nc}^{(\ell)}(G,v),\,\{\!\{{\sf nc}^{(\ell)}(G,u)\mid u\in N(v)\}\!\},
{{(𝗇𝖼(ℓ)(G,u),𝗇𝖼(ℓ)(G,w))∣u,w∈N(v),{u,w}∈E}}).\displaystyle\,\,\,\{\!\{({\sf nc}^{(\ell)}(G,u),{\sf nc}^{(\ell)}(G,w))\mid u,w\in N(v),\,\{u,w\}\in E\}\!\}\big).

In other words, besides taking into account the multiset of colors of the neighbors of a vertex vv, as in 1WL, the NC-1WL test also considers the multiset of color pairs corresponding to the edges within the neighborhood of vv. We let 𝗇𝖼⁡(G,v){\sf nc}(G,v) denote the color of node vv once the coloring partition on vertices defined by the NC-1WL test becomes stable. We write 𝗇𝖼⁡(G){\sf nc}(G) for the multiset {{𝗇𝖼⁡(G,v)∣v∈V}}\{\!\{{\sf nc}(G,v)\mid v\in V\}\!\}, and call two graphs GG and G′G^{\prime} distinguishable by NC-1WL if 𝗇𝖼⁡(G)≠𝗇𝖼⁡(G′){\sf nc}(G)\neq{\sf nc}(G^{\prime}).

The additional structural information collected by NC-1WL makes it strictly more powerful than 1WL in distinguishing certain classes of non-isomorphic graphs. In turn, every pair of graphs that can be distinguished by NC-1WL can also be distinguished by 2WL, but the converse does not hold. The advantage of NC-1WL over 2WL, however, is that it achieves stronger discriminative power while still operating at the vertex level, in the same spirit as 1WL. In particular, its computational cost is closer to that of 1WL than to the more demanding 2WL procedure.

3 Edge-based WL test

In this section, we introduce the EB-1WL test (for edge-based 1WL), an extension of 1WL and NC-1WL that colors edges rather than vertices—analogous to higher-order WL tests that color vertex tuples. Unlike those tests, EB-1WL colors only edge pairs, reducing space complexity from quadratic in nodes to linear in edges and making it more practical. By focusing on edges, EB-1WL gains greater expressive power than NC-1WL while maintaining reasonable computational cost.

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be an undirected graph. We iteratively associate a color 𝖾𝖻(ℓ)​(G,(u,v)){\sf eb}^{(\ell)}(G,(u,v)) with each ordered pair (u,v)(u,v) such that {u,v}∈E\{u,v\}\in E. That is, each edge receives two colors, one for each ordering of its endpoints. The coloring of the ordered pair (u,v)(u,v) is defined inductively. Initially, every pair has the same color: 𝖾𝖻(0)​(G,(u,v))=1{\sf eb}^{(0)}(G,(u,v))=1. At iteration ℓ+1\ell+1, the color of (u,v)(u,v) is updated according to

𝖾𝖻(ℓ+1)​(G,(u,v))=(CLOSE\displaystyle{\sf eb}^{(\ell+1)}(G,(u,v))=\Big(\, 𝖾𝖻(ℓ)​(G,(u,v)),\displaystyle{\sf eb}^{(\ell)}(G,(u,v)), (1)
{{𝖾𝖻(ℓ)(G,(u,x))∣x∈N(u)}} ,\displaystyle{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\bigl\{\!\!\bigl\{{\sf eb}^{(\ell)}(G,(u,x))\mid x\in N(u)\bigl\}\!\!\bigl\}$}\hss}\color[rgb]{0.1172,0.5352,0.8984}\rule[-2.99998pt]{124.02002pt}{0.5pt}}, (2)
{{(𝖾𝖻(ℓ)(G,(u,y)),𝖾𝖻(ℓ)(G,(v,y)))∣y∈N(v)∩N(u)}} ,\displaystyle{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\bigl\{\!\!\bigl\{\left({\sf eb}^{(\ell)}(G,(u,y)),{\sf eb}^{(\ell)}(G,(v,y))\right)\mid y\in N(v)\cap N(u)\bigl\}\!\!\bigl\}$}\hss}\color[rgb]{1,0.7578,0.0273}\rule[-2.99998pt]{227.14882pt}{0.5pt}}, (3)
OPEN{{𝖾𝖻(ℓ)(G,(v,z))∣z∈N(v)}} ).\displaystyle{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\bigl\{\!\!\bigl\{{\sf eb}^{(\ell)}(G,(v,z))\mid z\in N(v)\bigl\}\!\!\bigl\}$}\hss}\color[rgb]{0.8477,0.1055,0.375}\rule[-2.99998pt]{121.73294pt}{0.5pt}}\Big). (4)

This update rule refines the color of an edge based on the colors of edges incident to its endpoints as can be seen in Fig. 1. Eq. (2) captures the influence of edges incident to uu, Eq. (4) does the same for edges incident to vv, and Eq. (3) encodes the interaction between edges that are incident to both uu and vv, thereby forming a triangle and incorporating the local neighborhood structure around the edge.

We let 𝖾𝖻⁡(G,(u,v)){\sf eb}(G,(u,v)) denote the color of the ordered pair (u,v)(u,v) once the coloring partition of the edges defined by the NC-1WL test becomes stable. We write 𝖾𝖻⁡(G){\sf eb}(G) for the multiset {{𝖾𝖻(G,(u,v)),𝖾𝖻(G,(v,u))∣{u,v}∈E}}\{\!\{{\sf eb}(G,(u,v)),{\sf eb}(G,(v,u))\mid\{u,v\}\in E\}\!\} and call two graphs GG and G′G^{\prime} distinguishable by EB-1WL if they have a different number of vertices or 𝖾𝖻⁡(G)≠𝖾𝖻⁡(G′){\sf eb}(G)\neq{\sf eb}(G^{\prime}).

Computational cost of EB-1WL. Next, we study the computational cost of EB-1WL. We consider an idealized computational model where a multiset of ss elements can be created in time O⁡(s)O(s) and stored in O⁡(1)O(1) space (in practice, this can be achieved with high probability using hashing). In this model, we need O⁡(m)O(m) space to store the graph and the colors of the edges.

Now we analyze the time needed to perform a single iteration. First, computing the multisets in Eq.s (2) and (4) for all nodes uu and vv can be done in total time O⁡(m)O(m), since for every node uu (and, resp., vv) we spend time proportional to its degree. The more interesting part is computing Eq. (3) efficiently for all ordered edges (u,v)(u,v). For this, we need to go through all common neighbors yy of uu and vv. A naïve approach would iterate over all neighbors yy of uu and then check whether (y,v)(y,v) exists. This becomes slow if uu has a much higher degree than vv, potentially taking total time O⁡(m​d)O(md), where dd is the maximum degree of the graph. Instead, if we iterate only over the neighbors of the lower-degree node of uu and vv, then the analysis of the algorithm by Chiba & Nishizeki (1985) implies a running time of O⁡(α​m)O(\alpha m), where α\alpha is the arboricity of the graph, which is typically much smaller than the maximum degree. In practice, this ensures that EB1-WL runs in near-linear time per iteration. Thus, we get the following proposition.

Proposition 1.

An iteration of EB-1WL can be performed using O⁡(m)O(m) space and O⁡(α​m)O(\alpha m) time.

Comparing with the NC-1WL architecture, one can note that although this architecture requires just O⁡(n)O(n) space to store colors, it still requires O⁡(m)O(m) for storing the graph, providing no advantage over EB-1WL. Similarly, the NC-1WL architecture requires going through all triangles of the graph, and we are not aware of any algorithm that does this faster than in O⁡(α​m)O(\alpha m) time.

4 The distinguishing power of EB-1WL

4.1 Expressivity

We first observe that the EB-1WL test is at least as expressive as the NC-1WL test, and consequently also at least as expressive as the classical 1WL test, in distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs. Moreover, EB-1WL is strictly more expressive than NC-1WL for distinguishing graphs.

Proposition 2.

Every pair of graphs distinguishable by NC-1WL is also distinguishable by EB-1WL.

Proof.

Fix a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) (we omit GG in the notation for colors from now on). In the proof, we use the following terminology. An “ordered edge” is an ordered pair of nodes, connected by an edge (EB-1WL assigns colors to ordered edges). Now, an “ordered triangle” is an ordered triple of nodes where all nodes are connected by an edge.

To simplify the presentation, we will also use the following notation. For example, if uu is a node of GG, then (u,∗)(u,*) is the set of ordered pairs of nodes connected by an edge, where the first node in the pair is uu. Likewise, (∗,u)(*,u) will be a similar set but for pairs where the second node is uu.

More generally, if we have a kk-tuple where some coordinates are nodes of GG, and some coordinates are ∗* (meaning “undefined’), this tuple denotes the set of all ways to replace ∗*’s by nodes of GG such that all pairs of nodes in the tuple are connected by an edge. For example, (∗,∗,∗)(*,*,*) means the set of all ordered triangles, and (u,∗,∗)(u,*,*) denotes the set of all ordered triangles that have uu as the first coordinate.

Next, if cc is a coloring of nodes, and tt is a tuple of nodes, we will write c⁡(t)c(t) for the tuple of colors of nodes in tt, for instance, if t=(u,v,w)t=(u,v,w), then c⁡(t)=(c⁡(u),c⁡(v),c⁡(w))c(t)=(c(u),c(v),c(w)). Likewise, if cc is a coloring of pairs of nodes, and tt is a tuple, then we will write c⁡(t)c(t) for the tuple of colors of all pairs of nodes in tt. We will use this when tt is at most a triple of nodes, where then it is defined as:

c⁡(u,v,w)=(c⁡(u,v),c⁡(u,w),c⁡(v,w)).c(u,v,w)=(c(u,v),c(u,w),c(v,w)).

Moreover, we extend this notation to tuples with ∗*s. Namely, if TT is a tuple of with stars (a set of tuples of nodes without starts), then c(T)={{c(t)∣t∈T}}c(T)=\bigl\{\!\!\bigl\{c(t)\mid t\in T\bigl\}\!\!\bigl\}.

In this notation, the updates of NC-1WL and EB-1WL can be defined as follows. The color n​c(ℓ+1)​(u)nc^{(\ell+1)}(u) is defined by multisets n​c(ℓ+1)​(u,∗)nc^{(\ell+1)}(u,*) and n​c(ℓ+1)​(u,∗,∗)nc^{(\ell+1)}(u,*,*). In turn, the color 𝖾𝖻(ℓ+1)​(u,v){\sf eb}^{(\ell+1)}(u,v) is defined by 𝖾𝖻(ℓ)​(u,∗){\sf eb}^{(\ell)}(u,*), 𝖾𝖻(ℓ)​(v,∗){\sf eb}^{(\ell)}(v,*), and 𝖾𝖻(ℓ)(u,v,∗){\sf eb}^{(\ell)}(u,v,*).

To establish the proposition, it is enough to show that 𝖾𝖻⁡(∗,∗){\sf eb}(*,*) uniquely determines 𝗇𝖼(ℓ)​(∗){\sf nc}^{(\ell)}(*) for every ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0.

Lemma 1.

For every ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0, and for every ordered edge (u,v)(u,v), we have that 𝖾𝖻⁡(u,v){\sf eb}(u,v) uniquely determines 𝗇𝖼(ℓ)​(u){\sf nc}^{(\ell)}(u) and 𝗇𝖼(ℓ)​(v){\sf nc}^{(\ell)}(v).

Proof.

The proof is by induction on ℓ\ell. For ℓ=0\ell=0, all nodes have the same 𝗇𝖼(0){\sf nc}^{(0)}-color, so there is nothing to prove. Assume now that the statement is proved for ℓ\ell, we establish it for ℓ+1\ell+1. That is, we have to show that 𝖾𝖻⁡(u,v){\sf eb}(u,v) uniquely determines 𝗇𝖼(ℓ+1)​(u){\sf nc}^{(\ell+1)}(u) and 𝗇𝖼(ℓ+1)​(v){\sf nc}^{(\ell+1)}(v). We only show that it determines 𝗇𝖼(ℓ+1)​(u){\sf nc}^{(\ell+1)}(u). It is enough because by induction in (1–4), it can be shown that 𝖾𝖻⁡(u,v){\sf eb}(u,v) uniquely determines 𝖾𝖻⁡(v,u){\sf eb}(v,u).

By definition, 𝖾𝖻(ℓ)​(u,v){\sf eb}^{(\ell)}(u,v) uniquely determines 𝖾𝖻(ℓ−1)​(u,∗){\sf eb}^{(\ell-1)}(u,*) and 𝖾𝖻(ℓ−1)(u,v,∗){\sf eb}^{(\ell-1)}(u,v,*). If we make one more step, from 𝖾𝖻(ℓ−1)​(u,∗){\sf eb}^{(\ell-1)}(u,*) we can determine 𝖾𝖻(ℓ−2)​(u,∗,∗){\sf eb}^{(\ell-2)}(u,*,*). Indeed, we use the fact that we can determine 𝖾𝖻(ℓ−2)(u,w,∗){\sf eb}^{(\ell-2)}(u,w,*) from 𝖾𝖻(ℓ−1)​(u,w){\sf eb}^{(\ell-1)}(u,w) for (u,w)∈(u,∗)(u,w)\in(u,*).

For a stable EB-1WL coloring 𝖾𝖻{\sf eb}, we thus get that 𝖾𝖻⁡(u,v){\sf eb}(u,v) uniquely determines 𝖾𝖻⁡(u,∗){\sf eb}(u,*) and 𝖾𝖻⁡(u,∗,∗){\sf eb}(u,*,*). They, in turn, by the induction hypothesis, uniquely determined 𝗇𝖼ℓ​(u,∗){\sf nc}^{\ell}(u,*) and 𝗇𝖼ℓ​(u,∗,∗){\sf nc}^{\ell}(u,*,*). Thus, from this information, we get 𝗇𝖼(ℓ+1)​(u){\sf nc}^{(\ell+1)}(u), as required. ∎

We now finish the proof of the proposition. Assume that we want to know how many times a node color cc appears in 𝗇𝖼(ℓ)​(∗){\sf nc}^{(\ell)}(*). We can assume that ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 (we can determine the multiset for ℓ=0\ell=0 from the multiset for ℓ=1\ell=1), then the color cc uniquely determines the degree dd of a node (which is not 0 by the assumption of the absence of isolated nodes). We go through all ordered edges (u,v)(u,v) and count how many times we have 𝗇𝖼(ℓ)​(u)=c{\sf nc}^{(\ell)}(u)=c. We count every node dd times, so we have to divide this number by dd. ∎

Theorem 1.

The graphs GG and HH in Fig. 3 can be distinguished by EB-1WL but not by NC-1WL. That is, EB-1WL is strictly more expressive than NC-1WL and 1WL.

Proof.

The graphs GG and HH are given in Fig. 3. Both have 16 nodes and are based on the 16-gons. The graph GG has also all chords for vertices at distance 2 and at distance 4 in the 16-gon. In turn, the graph HH has all chords for vertices at distance 3 and distance 4 in the 16-gon.

All nodes in both graphs have degree 6. Moreover, all nodes in both graphs appear in the same number of triangles, namely, 6. Indeed, every triangle in both graphs is given by an equation a+b=ca+b=c, for some chords, connecting vertices at distances a,ba,b and cc, respectively. In the first graph, there are two types of triangles, 1+1=21+1=2 and 2+2=42+2=4. Each type, when we rotate it over the 16-gon, covers each vertex exactly 3 times, giving 6 triangles for each node. In the second graph, there are also two types of triangles, 1+3=41+3=4 and 3+1=43+1=4 (differing just by their orientation), so the same count gives 6 triangles for every node.

This implies that the NC-1WL gives the same color to all nodes of both graphs in the first iteration, and thus, cannot distinguish these two graphs.

On the other hand, these two graphs can be distinguished by the EB-1WL. Indeed, in HH, every edge appears in 2 triangles (every 1-edge or every 3-edge we can complement either from the left or from the right, and every 4-edge we can complete in two ways inside). But, say, for the 4-edge in the first graph, there is just one 2 + 2 triangle that has it. ∎

Similar to NC-1WL, any pair of graphs distinguishable by EB-1WL is also distinguishable by 2WL, though the reverse implication does not hold. A concrete example of a pair of graphs that is distinguishable by 2WL but neither by EB-1WL nor NC-1WL is shown in Fig. 3.

4.2 Logical characterization

The distinguishing power of the kk-WL test can be characterized via a fragment of first-order logic, namely the (k+1)(k+1)-variable fragment with counting quantifiers (Cai et al., 1992), with 1WL and 2WL corresponding to the two- and three-variable fragments, respectively. These logical characterizations have been an important tool in studying GNNs, as they offer helpful insights into what GNNs can accomplish. We show that EB-1WL also admits a natural logical characterization, further demonstrating the robustness and naturalness of our newly proposed framework. Specifically, EB-1WL corresponds to a novel natural logic we introduce below. This logic lies strictly between the two- and three-variable counting fragments, providing a precise conceptualization of its position “between” 1WL and 2WL.

We assume familiarity with the syntax and semantics of first-order logic (FO). We write ϕ⁡(x¯)\phi(\bar{x}) to indicate that the free variables of ϕ\phi are exactly those in the tuple x¯\bar{x}. When interpreted over graphs, FO formulas are defined over a vocabulary consisting of a single binary relation symbol EE. Specifically, the formula E⁡(x,y)E(x,y) is interpreted over a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) as the set of all pairs (u,v)∈V×V(u,v)\in V\times V such that {u,v}∈E\{u,v\}\in E. Given a tuple x¯=(x1,…,xn)\bar{x}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) of distinct variables, we define the FO formula

𝖼𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾⁡(x¯):=⋀1≤i<j≤nE⁡(xi,xj),{\sf clique}(\bar{x})\ :=\ \bigwedge_{1\leq i<j\leq n}E(x_{i},x_{j}),

so that its interpretation over GG is the set of all nn-tuples of vertices that form a clique in GG.

We now introduce our novel clique-based first-order logic with counting (CFOC) via the following syntax:

  1. 1.

    If x¯\bar{x} is a tuple of distinct variables, then 𝖼𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾⁡(x¯){\sf clique}(\bar{x}) is a formula in CFOC.

  2. 2.

    If ϕ⁡(x¯)\phi(\bar{x}) is a formula in CFOC, then so is 𝖼𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾⁡(x¯)∧¬ϕ⁡(x¯){\sf clique}(\bar{x})\wedge\neg\phi(\bar{x}).

  3. 3.

    If ϕ⁡(x¯)\phi(\bar{x}) and ψ⁡(y¯)\psi(\bar{y}) are formulas in CFOC, then so is 𝖼𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾⁡(z¯)∧(ϕ⁡(x¯)⋆ψ⁡(y¯)){\sf clique}(\bar{z})\wedge(\phi(\bar{x})\star\psi(\bar{y})) for any ⋆∈{∧,∨}\star\in\{\wedge,\vee\}, where z¯\bar{z} is is the tuple obtained by collecting all variables that occur in x¯\bar{x} and y¯\bar{y}, removing any duplicates, so that each variable appears exactly once.

  4. 4.

    If ϕ⁡(x¯,y)\phi(\bar{x},y) is a formula in CFOC, then 𝖼𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾⁡(x¯)∧∃≥ky​ϕ​(x¯,y){\sf clique}(\bar{x})\wedge\exists^{\geq k}y\,\phi(\bar{x},y) is a formula in CFOC, for any integer k≥1k\geq 1, where the semantics of ∃≥ky​ϕ​(x¯,y)\exists^{\geq k}y\,\phi(\bar{x},y) assert that there exist at least kk vertices vv such that ϕ⁡(x¯,y)\phi(\bar{x},y) holds when y=vy=v.

Intuitively, CFOC restricts FO with counting quantifiers to formulas whose free variables form a clique in the graph. We note that this is reminiscent of, but not directly related to, the so-called clique-guarded fragments of first-order logic; see, e.g., Grädel (1999).

We denote CFOC3 the fragment of CFOC that consists of formulas that use at most three variables. For example, the CFOC3 formula ψ:=∃≥1x​∃≥1y⁡(𝖼𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾⁡(x,y)∧∃≥3z​𝖼𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾​(x,y,z))\psi:=\exists^{\geq 1}x\exists^{\geq 1}y\ \big(\,{\sf clique}(x,y)\land\exists^{\geq 3}z\,{\sf clique}(x,y,z)\,\big) checks if there is an edge which is a part of at least 3 triangles. A CFOC3 sentence is a CFOC3 formula without free variables. We call graphs GG and HH distinguishable by CFOC3, if there is a CFOC3 sentence ϕ\phi such that G⊧ϕG\models\phi but H⊧̸ϕH\not\models\phi.

Example 1.

The sentence ψ\psi shown above holds in graph HH from Figure 3, but not in graph GG. ▲\blacktriangle

We can now establish our characterization:

Theorem 2.

The pairs of graphs that are distinguishable by EB-1WL are precisely those that are distinguishable by CFOC3{\rm CFOC}^{3}.

Proof.

We start by showing the following.

Lemma 2.

For each possible color cc that the EB-1WL test obtains after tt rounds, there is a formula ϕc​(x,y)\phi_{c}(x,y) of quantifier depth tt in CFOC3 such that 𝖾𝖻t​(G,(u,v))=c{\sf eb}^{t}(G,(u,v))=c if and only if G⊧ϕc​(u,v)G\models\phi_{c}(u,v), for each graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) and edge {u,v}∈E\{u,v\}\in E.

Proof.

We prove the result by induction on the number of rounds t≥0t\geq 0. By definition of EB-1WL, before any refinement every edge {u,v}\{u,v\} receives the same initial color c=1c=1. Accordingly, we can define ϕc​(x,y):=E⁡(x,y)\phi_{c}(x,y)\ :=\ E(x,y).

Suppose we already have, for every color dd occurring after tt rounds of EB-1WL, a formula ϕd​(x,y)\phi_{d}(x,y) that defines it. Consider now a new color cc obtained after t+1t+1 rounds. By the definition of EB-1WL, the color of an edge {u,v}\{u,v\} at step t+1t+1 is completely determined by the following information from step tt:

  1. 1.

    the color dd previously assigned to {u,v}\{u,v\},

  2. 2.

    the multiset ℰ\mathcal{E} of colors of edges of the form {u,w}\{u,w\},

  3. 3.

    the multiset 𝒢\mathcal{G} of colors of edges of the form {v,w}\{v,w\}, and

  4. 4.

    the multiset ℱ\mathcal{F} of pairs of colors (f1,f2)(f_{1},f_{2}) corresponding to edges {u,w}\{u,w\} and {v,w}\{v,w\} incident with a common neighbor ww.

It follows that the new color cc can be described in CFOC3 by the formula:

ϕc​(x,y)\displaystyle\phi_{c}(x,y)\ :=ϕd​(x,y)∧\displaystyle:=\ \phi_{d}(x,y)\,\wedge
⋀e∈ℰ∃=nez⁡(E⁡(x,z)∧ϕe​(x,z))∧∃=∑e∈ℰnez​E​(x,z)\displaystyle\bigwedge_{e\in{\cal E}}\exists^{=n_{e}}z\big(E(x,z)\wedge\phi_{e}(x,z)\big)\,\wedge\,\exists^{=\sum_{e\in{\cal E}}n_{e}}zE(x,z)
⋀g∈𝒢∃=mgz⁡(E⁡(z,y)∧ϕg​(z,y))∧∃=∑g∈𝒢mgz​E​(y,z)\displaystyle\bigwedge_{g\in{\cal G}}\exists^{=m_{g}}z\big(E(z,y)\wedge\phi_{g}(z,y)\big)\,\wedge\,\exists^{=\sum_{g\in{\cal G}}m_{g}}zE(y,z)
⋀(f1,f2)∈ℱ∃=p(f1,f2)z⁡(E⁡(x,z)∧E⁡(y,z)∧ϕf1​(x,z)∧ϕf2​(y,z))∧\displaystyle\bigwedge_{(f_{1},f_{2})\in{\cal F}}\exists^{=p_{(f_{1},f_{2})}}z\big(E(x,z)\wedge E(y,z)\wedge\phi_{f_{1}}(x,z)\wedge\phi_{f_{2}}(y,z)\big)\,\wedge
∃=∑(f1,f2)∈ℱp(f1,f2)z⁡(E⁡(x,z)∧E⁡(y,z)).\displaystyle\exists^{=\sum_{(f_{1},f_{2})\in{\cal F}}p_{(f_{1},f_{2})}}z\big(E(x,z)\wedge E(y,z)\big).

Here, nen_{e} is the multiplicity of ee in ℰ\mathcal{E}, mgm_{g} the multiplicity of gg in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, and p(f1,f2)p_{(f_{1},f_{2})} the multiplicity of (f1,f2)(f_{1},f_{2}) in ℱ\mathcal{F}. As usual, we write ∃=nx​ψ\exists^{=n}x\,\psi as shorthand for ∃≥nx​ψ∧¬∃≥n+1x​ψ\exists^{\geq n}x\,\psi\ \wedge\ \neg\exists^{\geq n+1}x\,\psi. Notice that ϕc​(x,y)\phi_{c}(x,y) has quantifier rank t+1t+1. ∎

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a graph and v¯\bar{v} a tuple of elements in VV. For t≥0t\geq 0, we write 𝗍𝗉t​(G,v¯){\sf tp}^{t}(G,\bar{v}) for the tt-type of (G,v¯)(G,\bar{v}), which is the set of formulas ϕ⁡(x¯)\phi(\bar{x}) with quantifier depth tt in CFOC3 such that G⊧ϕ⁡(v¯)G\models\phi(\bar{v}). Also, 𝖾𝖻t​(G){\sf eb}^{t}(G) is the multiset formed by all elements of the form 𝖾𝖻t​(G,(u,v)){\sf eb}^{t}(G,(u,v)), where {u,v}∈E\{u,v\}\in E.

Lemma 3.

Consider graphs G=(V,E)G=(V,E) and G′=(V′,E′)G^{\prime}=(V^{\prime},E^{\prime}) and edges {u,v}∈E\{u,v\}\in E and {u′,v′}∈E′\{u^{\prime},v^{\prime}\}\in E^{\prime}. Then for each t≥0t\geq 0, the following hold:

  1. 1.

    If 𝖾𝖻t​(G)=𝖾𝖻t​(G′){\sf eb}^{t}(G)={\sf eb}^{t}(G^{\prime}) then 𝗍𝗉t​(G)=𝗍𝗉t​(G′){\sf tp}^{t}(G)={\sf tp}^{t}(G^{\prime}).

  2. 2.

    If 𝖾𝖻t​(G,(u,v))=𝖾𝖻t​(G′,(u′,v′)){\sf eb}^{t}(G,(u,v))={\sf eb}^{t}(G^{\prime},(u^{\prime},v^{\prime})) and 𝖾𝖻t​(G)=𝖾𝖻t​(G′){\sf eb}^{t}(G)={\sf eb}^{t}(G^{\prime}), then 𝗍𝗉t​(G,u)=𝗍𝗉t​(G′,u′){\sf tp}^{t}(G,u)={\sf tp}^{t}(G^{\prime},u^{\prime}), 𝗍𝗉t​(G,v)=𝗍𝗉t​(G′,v′){\sf tp}^{t}(G,v)={\sf tp}^{t}(G^{\prime},v^{\prime}), and 𝗍𝗉t​(G,(u,v))=𝗍𝗉t​(G′,(u′,v′)){\sf tp}^{t}(G,(u,v))={\sf tp}^{t}(G^{\prime},(u^{\prime},v^{\prime})).

Proof.

We prove this by induction on t≥0t\geq 0. The base case t=0t=0 holds trivially. In fact, there are no sentences in CFOC3 of quantifier depth 00, and hence 𝗍𝗉0​(G)=𝗍𝗉0​(G′){\sf tp}^{0}(G)={\sf tp}^{0}(G^{\prime}) holds vacuously. Moreover, any formula ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) of quantifier depth 00 with only one free variable xx in CFOC3 is a Boolean combination of formulas of the form E⁡(x,x)E(x,x). Since both G⊧¬E⁡(u,u)G\models\neg E(u,u) and G′⊧¬E⁡(u′,u′)G^{\prime}\models\neg E(u^{\prime},u^{\prime}), it is the case that G⊧ϕ⁡(u)⇔G′⊧ϕ⁡(u′)G\models\phi(u)\Leftrightarrow G^{\prime}\models\phi(u^{\prime}). The same holds for vv. Finally, any formula ϕ⁡(x,y)\phi(x,y) of quantifier depth 00 with only two free variables xx and yy in CFOC3 is a Boolean combination of formulas of the form E⁡(x,y)E(x,y), E⁡(x,x)E(x,x), and E⁡(y,y)E(y,y). Since both G⊧¬E⁡(u,u)G\models\neg E(u,u) and G′⊧¬E⁡(u′,u′)G^{\prime}\models\neg E(u^{\prime},u^{\prime}), both G⊧¬E⁡(v,v)G\models\neg E(v,v) and G′⊧¬E⁡(v′,v′)G^{\prime}\models\neg E(v^{\prime},v^{\prime}), and both G⊧E⁡(u,v)G\models E(u,v) and G′⊧¬E⁡(u′,v′)G^{\prime}\models\neg E(u^{\prime},v^{\prime}), it is the case that G⊧ϕ⁡(u,v)⇔G′⊧ϕ⁡(u′,v′)G\models\phi(u,v)\Leftrightarrow G^{\prime}\models\phi(u^{\prime},v^{\prime}).

Let us consider now the inductive case t+1t+1, for t≥0t\geq 0. We prove (1) and (2) separately.

Proof of (1): Assume that 𝖾𝖻t+1​(G)=𝖾𝖻t+1​(G′){\sf eb}^{t+1}(G)={\sf eb}^{t+1}(G^{\prime}). Consider a sentence ϕ\phi in CFOC3 of quantifier depth t+1t+1. First, note that the case t=0t=0 is trivial: in this situation, ϕ\phi must be a Boolean combination of formulas of the form ∃≥nx​ψ​(x)\exists^{\geq n}x\,\psi(x), where ψ⁡(x)\psi(x) is itself a Boolean combination of formulas of the form E⁡(x,x)E(x,x). Consequently, either every graph GG satisfies ϕ\phi or none does.

Now assume t>0t>0, and let ϕ\phi be a Boolean combination of CFOC3 formulas of the form ∃≥nx​ϕ​(x)\exists^{\geq n}x\,\phi(x), where ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) has quantifier depth tt. Our assumption 𝖾𝖻t+1​(G)=𝖾𝖻t+1​(G′){\sf eb}^{t+1}(G)={\sf eb}^{t+1}(G^{\prime}) implies

{{𝖾𝖻t​(G,(u,v))∣{u,v}∈E}}={{𝖾𝖻t​(G′,(u′,v′))∣{u′,v′}∈E′}},\{\!\{{\sf eb}^{t}(G,(u,v))\mid\{u,v\}\in E\}\!\}=\{\!\{{\sf eb}^{t}(G^{\prime},(u^{\prime},v^{\prime}))\mid\{u^{\prime},v^{\prime}\}\in E^{\prime}\}\!\},

{{𝗍𝗉t​(G,(u,v))∣{u,v}∈E}}={{𝗍𝗉t​(G′,(u′,v′))∣{u′,v′}∈E′}}.\{\!\{{\sf tp}^{t}(G,(u,v))\mid\{u,v\}\in E\}\!\}=\{\!\{{\sf tp}^{t}(G^{\prime},(u^{\prime},v^{\prime}))\mid\{u^{\prime},v^{\prime}\}\in E^{\prime}\}\!\}.

Moreover, 𝗍𝗉t​(G,(u,v)){\sf tp}^{t}(G,(u,v)) determines both 𝗍𝗉t​(G,u){\sf tp}^{t}(G,u) and 𝗍𝗉t​(G,v){\sf tp}^{t}(G,v).

|S⁡(G,τ)|/dand|S⁡(G′,τ)|/d,|S(G,\tau)|/d\quad\text{and}\quad|S(G^{\prime},\tau)|/d,

respectively. Because S⁡(G,τ)=S⁡(G′,τ)S(G,\tau)=S(G^{\prime},\tau) by the above, the two counts coincide, which completes the proof.

{{(𝖾𝖻t(G,(u,w)),𝖾𝖻t(G,(v,w)))∣{u,w},{v,w}∈E}}={{(𝖾𝖻t(G′,(u′,w′)),𝖾𝖻t(G′,(v′,w)))∣{u′,w′},{v′,w′}∈E′}}.\{\!\{\big({\sf eb}^{t}(G,(u,w)),{\sf eb}^{t}(G,(v,w))\big)\mid\{u,w\},\{v,w\}\in E\}\!\}\ =\\ \{\!\{\big({\sf eb}^{t}(G^{\prime},(u^{\prime},w^{\prime})),{\sf eb}^{t}(G^{\prime},(v^{\prime},w))\big)\mid\{u^{\prime},w^{\prime}\},\{v^{\prime},w^{\prime}\}\in E^{\prime}\}\!\}.

Also by assumption, 𝖾𝖻t+1​(G)=𝖾𝖻t+1​(G′){\sf eb}^{t+1}(G)={\sf eb}^{t+1}(G^{\prime}), which implies that 𝖾𝖻t​(G)=𝖾𝖻t​(G′){\sf eb}^{t}(G)={\sf eb}^{t}(G^{\prime}). {{(𝗍𝗉t(G,(u,w)),𝗍𝗉t(G,(v,w)),𝗍𝗉t(G,w))∣{u,w},{v,w}∈E}}={{((𝗍𝗉t(G′,(u′,w′)),𝗍𝗉t(G′,(v′,w)),𝗍𝗉t(G′,w′))∣{u′,w′},{v′,w′}∈E′}}.\{\!\{\big({\sf tp}^{t}(G,(u,w)),{\sf tp}^{t}(G,(v,w)),{\sf tp}^{t}(G,w)\big)\mid\{u,w\},\{v,w\}\in E\}\!\}\ =\\ \{\!\{(\big({\sf tp}^{t}(G^{\prime},(u^{\prime},w^{\prime})),{\sf tp}^{t}(G^{\prime},(v^{\prime},w)),{\sf tp}^{t}(G^{\prime},w^{\prime})\big)\mid\{u^{\prime},w^{\prime}\},\{v^{\prime},w^{\prime}\}\in E^{\prime}\}\!\}.

This implies that

|{w∈N⁡(u)∩N⁡(v)∣G⊧β1​(u,v,w)}|=|{w′∈N⁡(u′)∩N⁡(v′)∣G′⊧β1​(u′,v′,w′)}|,|\{w\in N(u)\cap N(v)\mid G\models\beta_{1}(u,v,w)\}|=|\{w^{\prime}\in N(u^{\prime})\cap N(v^{\prime})\mid G^{\prime}\models\beta_{1}(u^{\prime},v^{\prime},w^{\prime})\}|,

which means that G⊧β⁡(u,v)⇔G′⊧β⁡(u′,v′)G\models\beta(u,v)\Leftrightarrow G^{\prime}\models\beta(u^{\prime},v^{\prime}).

Consider second a formula as above of the form γ⁡(x)\gamma(x). By construction, γ⁡(x)=∃≥nz⁡(E⁡(x,z)∧γ1​(x,z))\gamma(x)=\exists^{\geq n}z\,(E(x,z)\wedge\gamma_{1}(x,z)), where γ1​(x,z)\gamma_{1}(x,z) is a CFOC3 formula of quantifier depth tt. By assumption, 𝖾𝖻t+1​(G,(u,v))=𝖾𝖻t+1​(G′,(u′,v′)){\sf eb}^{t+1}(G,(u,v))={\sf eb}^{t+1}(G^{\prime},(u^{\prime},v^{\prime})), and hence

{{𝖾𝖻t​(G,(u,w))∣{u,w}∈E}}={{𝖾𝖻t​(G′,(u′,w′))∣{u′,w′}∈E′}}.\{\!\{{\sf eb}^{t}(G,(u,w))\mid\{u,w\}\in E\}\!\}\ =\ \{\!\{{\sf eb}^{t}(G^{\prime},(u^{\prime},w^{\prime}))\mid\{u^{\prime},w^{\prime}\}\in E^{\prime}\}\!\}.

By induction hypothesis, this implies that:

{{𝗍𝗉t​(G,(u,w))∣{u,w}∈E}}={{𝗍𝗉t​(G′,(u′,w′))∣{u′,w′}∈E′}}.\{\!\{{\sf tp}^{t}(G,(u,w))\mid\{u,w\}\in E\}\!\}\ =\ \{\!\{{\sf tp}^{t}(G^{\prime},(u^{\prime},w^{\prime}))\mid\{u^{\prime},w^{\prime}\}\in E^{\prime}\}\!\}.

By focusing on those types that contain γ1​(x,z)\gamma_{1}(x,z), we obtain:

|{w∈N⁡(u)∣G⊧γ1​(u,w)}|=|{w′∈N⁡(u′)∣G′⊧γ1​(u′,w′)}|,|\{w\in N(u)\mid G\models\gamma_{1}(u,w)\}|\ =\ |\{w^{\prime}\in N(u^{\prime})\mid G^{\prime}\models\gamma_{1}(u^{\prime},w^{\prime})\}|,

which means that G⊧γ⁡(u)⇔G′⊧γ⁡(u′)G\models\gamma(u)\Leftrightarrow G^{\prime}\models\gamma(u^{\prime}).

The formulas of the form δ⁡(y)\delta(y) are handled analogously to the previous case.

Finally, consider a sentence as above of the form η\eta. Since 𝖾𝖻t+1​(G)=𝖾𝖻t+1​(G′){\sf eb}^{t+1}(G)={\sf eb}^{t+1}(G^{\prime}), we have by part (1) that G⊧η⇔G′⊧ηG\models\eta\Leftrightarrow G^{\prime}\models\eta.

This finishes the proof of the lemma. ∎

We now prove Theorem 2. Assume first that 𝖾𝖻⁡(G)=𝖾𝖻⁡(G′){\sf eb}(G)={\sf eb}(G^{\prime}), for graphs GG and G′G^{\prime}. In particular, then, 𝖾𝖻t​(G)=𝖾𝖻t​(G′){\sf eb}^{t}(G)={\sf eb}^{t}(G^{\prime}) for every t≥0t\geq 0. Take an arbitrary sentence ϕ\phi of CFOC3, and assume that its quantifier depth is tt. From Lemma 3, we conclude that 𝗍𝗉t​(G)=𝗍𝗉t​(G′){\sf tp}^{t}(G)={\sf tp}^{t}(G^{\prime}), and hence G⊧ϕ⇔G⊧ϕ′G\models\phi\Leftrightarrow G\models\phi^{\prime}.

Assume, on the contrary, that G⊧ϕ⇔G⊧ϕ′G\models\phi\Leftrightarrow G\models\phi^{\prime}, for every CFOC3 sentence ϕ\phi. Hence, 𝗍𝗉t​(G)=𝗍𝗉t​(G′){\sf tp}^{t}(G)={\sf tp}^{t}(G^{\prime}) for every t≥0t\geq 0. To prove 𝖾𝖻⁡(G)=𝖾𝖻⁡(G′){\sf eb}(G)={\sf eb}(G^{\prime}) it suffices to show 𝖾𝖻t​(G)=𝖾𝖻t​(G′){\sf eb}^{t}(G)={\sf eb}^{t}(G^{\prime}) for each t≥0t\geq 0. For a node v∈Vv\in V, define 𝖾𝖻t​(v)={{𝖾𝖻t​(v,w)∣{v,w}∈E}}{\sf eb}^{t}(v)=\{\!\{{\sf eb}^{t}(v,w)\mid\{v,w\}\in E\}\!\}. Notice, then, that 𝖾𝖻t​(G){\sf eb}^{t}(G) is completely determined by the multiset Γ⁡(G)={{𝖾𝖻t​(v)∣v∈V}}\Gamma(G)=\{\!\{{\sf eb}^{t}(v)\mid v\in V\}\!\}. For each element τ∈Γ⁡(G)\tau\in\Gamma(G), we write 𝒞τ{\cal C}_{\tau} for the multiset of colors computed by EB-1WL after tt steps that belong to τ\tau.

Define the following formula from CFOC3:

ϕG:=(⋀τ∈Γ⁡(G)∃=ℓτx​ϕτ​(x))∧∃=∑τ∈Γ⁡(G)ℓτx⁡(x=x),\phi_{G}:=\left(\bigwedge_{\tau\in\Gamma(G)}\exists^{=\ell_{\tau}}x\,\phi_{\tau}(x)\right)\,\wedge\,\exists^{=\sum_{\tau\in\Gamma(G)}\ell_{\tau}}x(x=x),

where ℓτ\ell_{\tau} is the multiplicity of τ\tau in Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) and ϕτ​(x)\phi_{\tau}(x) is defined as follows:

ϕτ​(x)=(⋀c∈𝒞τ∃=qcy⁡(E⁡(x,y)∧ϕc​(x,y)))∧∃=∑c∈𝒞τqτy​E​(x,y),\phi_{\tau}(x)\ =\ \left(\bigwedge_{c\in{\cal C}_{\tau}}\exists^{=q_{c}}y\,\big(E(x,y)\wedge\phi_{c}(x,y)\big)\right)\,\wedge\,\exists^{=\sum_{c\in{\cal C}_{\tau}}q_{\tau}}y\,E(x,y),

where qτq_{\tau} is the cardinality of τ\tau in Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) and ϕc​(x,y)\phi_{c}(x,y) is the CFOC3 formula from Lemma 2. Notice that ϕG\phi_{G} has quantifier depth bounded by t+2t+2.

It is easy to see that G′⊧ϕG⇔Γ⁡(G)=Γ⁡(G′)G^{\prime}\models\phi_{G}\Leftrightarrow\Gamma(G)=\Gamma(G^{\prime}). Since G⊧ϕGG\models\phi_{G} and 𝗍𝗉t+2​(G)=𝗍𝗉t+2​(G′){\sf tp}^{t+2}(G)={\sf tp}^{t+2}(G^{\prime}), we conclude that G′⊧ϕGG^{\prime}\models\phi_{G}, and hence Γ⁡(G)=Γ⁡(G′)\Gamma(G)=\Gamma(G^{\prime}). Since Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) determines 𝖾𝖻t​(G){\sf eb}^{t}(G), we conclude that 𝖾𝖻t​(G)=𝖾𝖻t​(G′){\sf eb}^{t}(G)={\sf eb}^{t}(G^{\prime}). ∎

4.3 Distinguishing power based on homomorphism counts

A central theme in the study of the WL test is its characterization via homomorphism counts. Formally, a homomorphism from a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) to a graph H=(V′,E′)H=(V^{\prime},E^{\prime}) is a mapping h:V→V′h:V\to V^{\prime} such that {h⁡(u),h⁡(v)}∈E′\{h(u),h(v)\}\in E^{\prime} for every edge {u,v}∈E\{u,v\}\in E. The connection between WL and homomorphism counts is as follows: two graphs are distinguishable by kkWL if and only if they differ in the number of homomorphisms from some graph of treewidth at most kk (Dvorák, 2010; Dell et al., 2018). For k=1k=1, this corresponds to the class of trees, and for k=2k=2 to the class of series-parallel graphs.

We show that distinguishability by EB-1WL is at least as powerful as distinguishing graphs by homomorphism counts from the class of chordal graphs of treewidth two, which strictly lies between the classes of graphs of treewidth one and two33 3 Note that, by definition, trees are always chordal.. Here, recall that a graph is chordal if it has no induced subgraph that is a cycle of length 4 or larger. This offers additional support for viewing EB-1WL as a natural and well-founded counterpart to the standard 1WL test.

Example 2.

Consider a graph JJ formed by two triangles sharing an edge. The graph JJ is a chordal graph of tree-width 2. Let GG and HH be the graphs from the proof of Theorem 1 that are distinguished by EB-1WL but not NC-1WL, see Fig. 3. We claim that the number of homomorhisms from JJ to GG is bigger then from JJ to HH. Indeed, observe that in HH every edge is in 2 triangles while in GG one third of the edges is in 1 triangle, one third is in 2 triangles, and one third is in 3 triangles. It remains to note that 4+4+4<1+4+94+4+4<1+4+9.

Theorem 3.

If two graphs have a different number of homomorphisms from some chordal graph of treewidth at most 2, they are distinguishable by EB-1WL.

Proof.

It is well-known that chordal graphs admit a perfect elimination order: an ordering of its nodes such that every node vv and its neighbors that go before vv in the order form a clique (Rose, 1970). Graphs of tree-width 2 cannot have cliques larger than a triangle; this means that for any chordal graph HH of tree-width 2 there exists an ordering v1,…,vmv_{1},\ldots,v_{m} of its nodes such that for any k∈{1,…,m}k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}, one of the following holds:

  • •

    (a) vkv_{k} is not connected to any node out of v1,…,vk−1v_{1},\ldots,v_{k-1};

  • •

    (b) vkv_{k} is connected to exactly one node out of v1,…,vk−1v_{1},\ldots,v_{k-1};

  • •

    (c) vkv_{k} is connected to exactly two nodes vi,vj∈{v1,…,vk−1}v_{i},v_{j}\in\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{k-1}\}, and viv_{i} and vjv_{j} are also connected.

Let 𝖾𝖻{\sf eb} be the stable EB-1WL coloring of GG. Let us show that the multiset 𝖾𝖻⁡(G){\sf eb}(G) of 𝖾𝖻{\sf eb}-labels of ordered edges uniquely determines the number of homomorphisms from HH to GG, for any tree-width 2 chordal graph HH. This means that if two graphs G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} have a different number of homomorphisms from some graph HH like that, they will be distinguished by the EB-1WL on the stage where colorings of both graphs stabilize.

For a node uu, define:

𝖾𝖻(u)={{𝖾𝖻(u,w)∣w∈N(u)}}.{\sf eb}(u)=\bigl\{\!\!\bigl\{{\sf eb}(u,w)\mid w\in N(u)\bigl\}\!\!\bigl\}.

Note that 𝖾𝖻⁡(u,v){\sf eb}(u,v), as it is stable, uniquely determines induced labels of uu and vv through (2) and (4). Moreover, 𝖾𝖻⁡(G){\sf eb}(G) uniquely determines the multiset 𝖾𝖻(V)={{𝖾𝖻(u)∣u∈V}}{\sf eb}(V)=\bigl\{\!\!\bigl\{{\sf eb}(u)\mid u\in V\bigl\}\!\!\bigl\}. Namely, we go through all 𝖾𝖻⁡(u,v){\sf eb}(u,v), compute 𝖾𝖻⁡(u){\sf eb}(u) from it, which in turn determines the degree of uu. We then divide the number of occurrences of 𝖾𝖻⁡(u){\sf eb}(u) by the degree.

Consider any labeling of edges of HH by labels from 𝖾𝖻⁡(G){\sf eb}(G), and of its nodes by labels from 𝖾𝖻⁡(V){\sf eb}(V). We show that for any such labeling, the number of homomorphisms from HH to GG that “preserve” this labeling is determined just by the multiset 𝖾𝖻⁡(G){\sf eb}(G). The total number of homomorphisms is hence also determined by 𝖾𝖻⁡(G){\sf eb}(G), since we can go through all possible labelings of HH and sum up homomorphisms for all of them.

Here, “preserve” formally means that (a) a node vjv_{j} with a label ℓ\ell goes into a node in GG that has this 𝖾𝖻{\sf eb}-label (b) if vi,vjv_{i},v_{j} is an edge of HH (where i<ji<j are indices of these nodes in the perfect elimination order), and if viv_{i} and vjv_{j} go to some nodes ui,uju_{i},u_{j} in GG, respectively, then the label of the edge vi,vjv_{i},v_{j} in HH has to be equal to 𝖾𝖻⁡(ui,uj){\sf eb}(u_{i},u_{j}).

We show that we can compute the number of homomorphisms that preserve a given labeling of HH, just knowing 𝖾𝖻⁡(G){\sf eb}(G), by first computing how many ways we can define the image of v1v_{1}, then the image of v2v_{2}, then of v3v_{3}, and so on.

As for v1v_{1}, it is assigned a label ℓ\ell in the labeling; we know the multiset of 𝖾𝖻{\sf eb}-labels of the nodes of GG, which determines the number of ways we can define the image of v1v_{1} (this is the number of nodes of GG that have label OPENℓ)\ell).

Now, assume that we have defined images of v1,…,vk−1v_{1},\ldots,v_{k-1}. Now, it’s vkv_{k}’s turn. Firstly, it is possible that vkv_{k} is not connected to any node among v1,…,vk−1v_{1},\ldots,v_{k-1}. Then we can freely map vkv_{k} to any node of GG that has the same label ℓ\ell as assigned to vkv_{k} in the coloring. We just have to multiply the current number of homomorphisms by the number of nodes in GG with this label ℓ\ell.

If vkv_{k} is connected to a single node viv_{i}, i<ki<k, and viv_{i} is already mapped to some node uiu_{i}, then we have to map vkv_{k} to some node uku_{k} that is connected to uiu_{i} and such that the 𝖾𝖻⁡(ui,uk){\sf eb}(u_{i},u_{k}) coincides with the color of the edge vi,vkv_{i},v_{k} in HH (this color also determines the label of uku_{k} which has to be consistent with the label that vkv_{k} has in the labeling of HH, otherwise the number of homomorphisms is just 00). The number of ways to choose such uku_{k} is thus determined by {{𝖾𝖻(ui,w)∣w∈N(ui)}}=𝖾𝖻(ui)\bigl\{\!\!\bigl\{{\sf eb}(u_{i},w)\mid w\in N({u_{i}})\bigl\}\!\!\bigl\}={\sf eb}(u_{i}), which in turn equals the label of viv_{i} in the labeling of HH. We multiply the current number of homomorphisms by the number of occurrences of the label of the edge vi,vkv_{i},v_{k} in the label of viv_{i}.

The same argument holds for the third case when vkv_{k} is connected to previous nodes vi,vjv_{i},v_{j} that are connected by an edge. The number of ways to choose the image of vkv_{k} is the number of occurrences of the pair (ℓi​k,ℓj​k)(\ell_{ik},\ell_{jk}) in (3) in the label of the edge ℓi​j\ell_{ij}, where ℓi​k,ℓj​k,\ell_{ik},\ell_{jk}, and ℓi​j\ell_{ij} are labels of edges vi,vkv_{i},v_{k}, vj,vkv_{j},v_{k}, and vi,vjv_{i},v_{j} in HH, respectively. ∎

5 Edge-based Graph Neural Networks

Now we introduce the EB-GNN architecture, a message-passing framework whose expressive power coincides with that of the EB-1WL test. Formally, a dd-dimensional EB-GNN 𝒯\mathcal{T} with t>0t>0 layers is specified by parameters ai,bi,ci,ui,vi∈ℝda_{i},b_{i},c_{i},u_{i},v_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and Ai,Ci,Ui,Vi∈ℝd×dA_{i},C_{i},U_{i},V_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, for i=1,…,ti=1,\ldots,t. Given a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), the EB-GNN 𝒯\mathcal{T} assigns to each ordered edge (u,v)(u,v) with {u,v}∈E\{u,v\}\in E and each layer 0≤i≤t0\leq i\leq t a feature vector f(i)​(u,v)∈ℝdf^{(i)}(u,v)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. At the input layer, we set44 4 When nodes or edges have additional input features, one can take them into account while defining f(0)​(u,v)f^{(0)}(u,v), see Section 6.

f(0)​(u,v)=(10…0)T∈ℝd.f^{(0)}(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&\ldots&0\end{pmatrix}^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (5)

For 1≤i≤t1\leq i\leq t, the update rules are given by

α(i)​(u)\alpha^{(i)}(u)  =∑x∈N⁡(u)ReLU⁡(Ai⋅f(i−1)​(u,x)+ai),\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in N(u)}\operatorname{ReLU}\!\Big(A_{i}\cdot f^{(i-1)}(u,x)+a_{i}\Big), (6)
β(i)​(u,v)\beta^{(i)}(u,v)  =∑y∈N⁡(u)∩N⁡(v)ReLU⁡(Bi⋅(f(i−1)​(u,y)f(i−1)​(v,y))+bi),\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in N(u)\cap N(v)}\operatorname{ReLU}\!\Big(B_{i}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}f^{(i-1)}(u,y)\\ f^{(i-1)}(v,y)\end{pmatrix}+b_{i}\Big), (7)
γ(i)​(v)\gamma^{(i)}(v)  =∑z∈N⁡(v)ReLU⁡(Ci⋅f(i−1)​(v,z)+ci),\displaystyle=\sum_{z\in N(v)}\operatorname{ReLU}\!\Big(C_{i}\cdot f^{(i-1)}(v,z)+c_{i}\Big), (8)
g(i)​(u,v)\displaystyle g^{(i)}(u,v) =f(i−1)​(u,v)+α(i)​(u)+β(i)​(u,v)+γ(i)​(v),\displaystyle=f^{(i-1)}(u,v)+\alpha^{(i)}(u)+\beta^{(i)}(u,v)+\gamma^{(i)}(v), (9)
f(i)​(u,v)\displaystyle f^{(i)}(u,v) =g(i)​(u,v)+FFNUi,ui,Vi,vi⁡(g(i)​(u,v)),\displaystyle=g^{(i)}(u,v)+\operatorname{FFN}_{U_{i},u_{i},V_{i},v_{i}}(g^{(i)}(u,v)), (10)

where ReLU⁡(x)=max⁡{0,x}\operatorname{ReLU}(x)=\max\{0,x\} is applied coordinate-wise in the equations above, and FFNU,u,V,v⁡(x)=V⋅ReLU⁡(U​x+u)+v\operatorname{FFN}_{U,u,V,v}(x)=V\cdot\operatorname{ReLU}(Ux+u)+v. The overall output of 𝒯\mathcal{T} on GG is defined as

𝒯⁡(G)=∑{u,v}∈Ef(t)​(u,v).\mathcal{T}(G)\;=\;\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}f^{(t)}(u,v). (11)

Graphs GG and HH are distinguishable by EB-GNNs if there exists an EB-GNN 𝒯\mathcal{T} with 𝒯⁡(G)≠𝒯⁡(H)\mathcal{T}(G)\neq\mathcal{T}(H).

It is immediate that the distinguishing power of EB-GNNs cannot exceed that of EB-1WL. Notably, we can show that this upper bound is tight.

Theorem 4.

Pairs of graphs distinguishable by EB-1WL are also distinguishable by EB-GNNs.

Proof.

The theorem is deduced from the following lemma.

Lemma 4.

Let f1,…,fn∈ℝdf_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be nn distinct vectors. Then there exists a matrix A∈ℝn×dA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} and a vector b∈ℝnb\in\mathbb{R}^{n} such that the vectors

g1=ReLU⁡(A​f1+b),…,gn=ReLU⁡(A​fn+b)g_{1}=\operatorname{ReLU}(Af_{1}+b),\ldots,g_{n}=\operatorname{ReLU}(Af_{n}+b)

are linearly independent.

Indeed, consider any two graphs GG and HH, distinguishable by the EB-1WL test. We construct an EB GNN 𝒯\mathcal{T} that distinguishes GG and HH.

Consider the disjoint union of GG and HH. Let mm be the number of ordered edges of this union, and tt be the number of ordered triangles. The dimension of 𝒯\mathcal{T} will be

d=1+2​m+t.d=1+2m+t.

We show that there exists a choice of parameter matrices such that, for any ii, a) EB-1WL labels after ii iterations are in a one-to-one correspondence with feature vectors f(i)​(u,v)f^{(i)}(u,v); b) all coordinates of f(i)f^{(i)}, except the first one, are 0s.

For i=0i=0, this holds because all edges initially have the same EB-1WL label, and because of (5).

Assume that it holds after i−1i-1 iterations. We use Lemma 4 in (6–8) to map distinct feature vectors f(i−1)​(u,v)f^{(i-1)}(u,v) (there are at most mm of them) or their pairs as in in (7)) (there are at most tt such pairs) to linearly independent vectors. This ensures that we obtain different sums for different multisets of terms in (6–8). We can use 3 blocks of m,mm,m and tt disjoint coordinates that are “‘free” in vectors f(i−1)​(u,v)f^{(i-1)}(u,v) so that the sum in (9) uniquely determines the whole 4-tuple in the definition of the updated EB-1WL feature.

We can then define a feed-forward network to injectively map vectors g(i)​(u,v)g^{(i)}(u,v) to vectors f(i)​(u,v)f^{(i)}(u,v) that have all coordinates, except the first one, equal to 00. There exists a vector w=(w1,…,wd)∈ℝdw=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{d} such that ⟨w,g(i)​(u,v)⟩≠⟨w,g(i)​(u′,v′)⟩\langle w,g^{(i)}(u,v)\rangle\neq\langle w,g^{(i)}(u^{\prime},v^{\prime})\rangle whenever g(i)​(u,v)≠g(i)​(u′,v′)g^{(i)}(u,v)\neq g^{(i)}(u^{\prime},v^{\prime}) (for each of the finitely many pairs of distinct g(i)g^{(i)}-vectors, the set of ww for which we have equality is a hyperplane in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}). Hence, it is enough to realize the following linear transformation by a FFN:

g(i)​(u,v)↦(w1w2…wd00…0⋱00…0)​g(i)​(u,v)=W​g(i)​(u,v).g^{(i)}(u,v)\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}w_{1}&w_{2}&\ldots&w_{d}\\ 0&0&\ldots&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ 0&0&\ldots&0\end{pmatrix}g^{(i)}(u,v)=Wg^{(i)}(u,v).

This can be achieved by the following FFN:

x↦W​ReLU⁡(x+ui)−W​ui,x\mapsto W\operatorname{ReLU}(x+u_{i})-Wu_{i},

where ui∈ℝdu_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is an arbitrary vector such that ui≥g(i)​(u,v)u_{i}\geq g^{(i)}(u,v) coordinate-wise for every ordered edge (u,v)(u,v). Indeed, then we obtain:

x↦W​ReLU⁡(x+ui)−W​ui=W⁡(x+ui)−W​ui=W​xx\mapsto W\operatorname{ReLU}(x+u_{i})-Wu_{i}=W(x+u_{i})-Wu_{i}=Wx

for any xx of the form x=g(i)​(u,v)x=g^{(i)}(u,v), as required.

Now, assume that we are at an iteration when GG and HH have different multisets of EB-1WL labels. We now need to to one more iteration that map distinct feature vectors into linearly independent vectors so that GG and HH will have different final representations in (11). We set all matrices and bias vectors in (6–8) to 0 so that g(i)​(u,v)=f(i−1)​(u,v)g^{(i)}(u,v)=f^{(i-1)}(u,v). We then use Lemma 4 again to construct a matrix UU and a vector uu such that the following transformation:

f(i−1)​(u,v)↦ReLU⁡(U​f(i−1)​(u,v)+v)f^{(i-1)}(u,v)\mapsto\operatorname{ReLU}(Uf^{(i-1)}(u,v)+v) (12)

maps distinct vectors into linearly independent ones. There are at most mm distinct feature vectors, which means we can use coordinates that are 0 in g(i)​(u,v)g^{(i)}(u,v) (by the invariant b)) for the image of (12) so it does not interfere with the first coordinate of g(i)​(u,v)g^{(i)}(u,v) in (10) . By setting V=I​d,v=0V=Id,v=0, we obtain a FFN that realizes this transformation.

Proof of Lemma 4.

Since f1,…,fnf_{1},\ldots,f_{n} are distinct, there exists w∈ℝdw\in\mathbb{R}^{d} such that ⟨f1,w⟩,…,⟨fn,w⟩\langle f_{1},w\rangle,\ldots,\langle f_{n},w\rangle are distinct (because the set of ww such that ⟨fi,w⟩=⟨fj,w⟩\langle f_{i},w\rangle=\langle f_{j},w\rangle for some i≠ji\neq j is a union of finitely many hyperplanes, not covering the whole ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}). Without loss of generality,

⟨f1,w⟩<⟨f2,w⟩<…<⟨fn,w⟩.\langle f_{1},w\rangle<\langle f_{2},w\rangle<\ldots<\langle f_{n},w\rangle.

For i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, let γi\gamma_{i} be some number between ⟨fi−1,w⟩\langle f_{i-1},w\rangle and ⟨fi,w⟩\langle f_{i},w\rangle (for i=1i=1, this is some number smaller than ⟨f1,w⟩\langle f_{1},w\rangle). Define

A=(ww),b=(−γ1−γ2−γn).A=\begin{pmatrix}w\\ \vdots\\ w\end{pmatrix},\qquad b=\begin{pmatrix}-\gamma_{1}\\ -\gamma_{2}\\ \vdots\\ -\gamma_{n}\end{pmatrix}.

Observe that in the vector

A​fi+b=(⟨fi,w⟩−γ1⟨fi,w⟩−γ2⟨fi,w⟩−γn)Af_{i}+b=\begin{pmatrix}\langle f_{i},w\rangle-\gamma_{1}\\ \langle f_{i},w\rangle-\gamma_{2}\\ \vdots\\ \langle f_{i},w\rangle-\gamma_{n}\end{pmatrix}

the first ii coordinates are strictly positive, and the other coordinates are strictly negative. Hence, the vector gi=ReLU⁡(A​fi+b)g_{i}=\operatorname{ReLU}(Af_{i}+b) is a vector where the first ii coordinates are strictly positive, and the rest are 0s. Therefore, g1,…,gng_{1},\ldots,g_{n} are linearly independent. ∎

This finishes the proof of the theorem. ∎

In our proof, EB-GNNs require dimension O⁡(m+t)O(m+t), where mm is the number of edges and tt the number of triangles. Whether this can be reduced to O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n), as shown for simulating 1WL by MPNNs (Aamand et al., 2022), remains open. Moreover, by replacing ReLU\operatorname{ReLU} with any analytic non-polynomial activation and concatenation in Eq. (7) with a Hadamard product, one can prove Thm. 4 already holds for d=1d=1, following techniques from Amir et al.; Bravo et al.; Hordan et al..

Algorithmic implementation.

In our implementation we perform a preprocessing step in which we enumerate all triangles in time O⁡(α​m)O(\alpha m) using the algorithm of  Chiba & Nishizeki (1985). Since each triangle (u,v,y)(u,v,y) corresponds to an edge (u,v)(u,v) and a node y∈N⁡(u)∩N⁡(v)y\in N(u)\cap N(v), we can obtain the sets N⁡(u)∩N⁡(v)N(u)\cap N(v) for all edges (u,v)(u,v) in time O⁡(α​m)O(\alpha m). After that, each iteration of EB-GNN takes time O⁡(m+t)O(m+t), where tt is the number of triangles—implying a better running time per iteration than in Proposition (1) because t=O⁡(m​α)t=O(m\alpha). However, due to this preprocessing step now we use memory O⁡(m+t)O(m+t) (instead of just O⁡(m)O(m)).

6 Experimental Evaluation

Now we empirically evaluate EB-GNN. The primary goal of our experiments is to show that EB-GNN provides a fast and expressive, general-purpose GNN architecture, and therefore we evaluate EB-GNN across tasks from diverse domains. We compare EB-GNN against Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs), another widely used general-purpose architecture, as well as against state-of-the-art models specifically optimized for each corresponding task. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/ocatias/EdgeBasedGNNs.

We focus on graph-level predictions and predictions on existing edges. While graph-level prediction tasks are a well-established use case for predictive GNNs (Morris et al., 2019; Paolino et al., 2024; Southern et al., 2025), prediction tasks on existing edges have received less attention. This latter task is relevant in chemistry: rather than relying on costly molecular simulations, GNNs can directly predict quantum mechanical properties, e.g., the bond length between atoms (Li et al., 2024).

6.1 Experiment setup

Next, we describe the datasets and baseline models used for comparison. We evaluate EB-GNN on two synthetic datasets designed to measure its practically realized expressivity. Additionally, we assess performance on three real-world datasets: two composed of small molecular graphs and one consisting of large cybersecurity graphs. Consistent with previous observations that real-world graphs have low arboricity, we find that these datasets exhibit small arboricity: ≤3\leq 3 for molecular graphs and ≤15\leq 15 for large cybersecurity graphs with each dataset having <4<4 mean arboricity. For each dataset, we compare EB-GNN against both general-purpose models and state-of-the-art task-specific baselines. Details on model and experiment setup are in App. A

Synthetic datasets for measuring expressivity.

We evaluate the empirical expressivity of EB-GNN on two synthetic datasets: CSL (Murphy et al., 2019; Dwivedi et al., 2023) and BREC (Wang & Zhang, 2024). The CSL dataset consists of 150 graphs with 41 nodes each, grouped into 10 distinct isomorphism classes. These classes, defined by skip connections between Hamiltonian cycles, are all indistinguishable by 11WL. The graph-level task is to classify each graph according to its isomorphism class. The BREC dataset comprises pairs of graphs that are indistinguishable by 11WL but distinguishable by 33WL. For each pair, the graph-level task is to compute embeddings that correctly differentiate the two graphs.

On the synthetic datasets, we compare EB-GNN against 22WL to assess how much of 22WL’s expressivity EB-GNN can replicate while maintaining asymptotically faster runtimes. In addition, we include a comparison with the MPNN GIN (Xu et al., 2019) augmented with triangle subgraph counts as node features (Bouritsas et al., 2022), referred to as MPNN + C3. This comparison helps isolate how much of EB-GNN’s expressivity gain stems from its ability to count triangles, as captured by the β\beta aggregation in Eq. (7).

Molecular edge-level and graph-level tasks.

We further evaluate EB-GNN on a range of molecular edge-level and graph-level prediction tasks.

Li et al. (2024) introduce the QMD dataset, which contains 65 000 molecular graphs annotated with various quantum mechanical properties. We assess EB-GNN on all four edge-level regression tasks from QMD. We evaluate four diverse graph-level regression tasks from QMD, selected to represent varied objectives (most other graph-level tasks in QMD focus on predicting HOMO/LUMO gaps).

We also evaluate EB-GNN on 12 graph-level regression tasks from the widely used QM9 dataset (Wu et al., 2018), following common practice (Morris et al., 2019; Paolino et al., 2024). QM9 comprises 130 000 molecular graphs representing molecules of up to 9 atoms. On average, graphs in both QMD and QM9 contain fewer than 20 nodes.

For QMD tasks, we compare EB-GNN against D-MPNN (Yang et al., 2019; Dai et al., 2016), a directed MPNN that has demonstrated strong performance on chemical prediction tasks (Vermeire et al., 2022; Heid & Green, 2022) and is integrated into the widely adopted ChemProp framework (Heid et al., 2024). Similar to EB-GNN, D-MPNN performs message passing on edges rather than nodes. For QM9, we compare against a standard MPNN and several expressive GNN architectures: 1-2-3 GNN (Morris et al., 2019), DTNN (Schütt et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2018), NestedGNN (Zhang & Li, 2021), I2-GNN (Huang et al., 2023), DRFWL (Zhou et al., 2023), and the recent state-of-the-art 5-ℓ\ellGIN baseline (Paolino et al., 2024).

Cybersecurity.

To evaluate our model on a different domain with larger graphs, we conduct experiments on MalNet-Tiny (Freitas et al., 2021). MalNet-Tiny consists of 5 000 graphs with an average of over 1 500 nodes, sampled from the MalNet dataset. The graph-level task is to classify whether a function call is benign or belongs to one of four malicious classes (AdWare, Trojan, Addisplay, Downloader). For comparison, we include a standard MPNN and the recently proposed subgraph GNN HyMN (Southern et al., 2025). We further compare against the graph transformer GPS (Rampášek et al., 2022) using different attention mechanisms: Performer (Choromanski et al., 2021), Big Bird (Zaheer et al., 2020), and the standard Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017).

6.2 Results

Recall that comparisons are made against both general-purpose MPNNs and state-of-the-art models for each dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that EB-GNN consistently outperforms standard MPNNs and remains competitive with state-of-the-art approaches.

Results on synthetic data.

Table 3 presents the results of our expressivity experiments on the synthetic datasets. On CSL, EB-GNN achieves an accuracy of 20%, outperforming a vanilla MPNN (10% accuracy) and matching an MPNN augmented with triangle counts (MPNN + C3, 20% accuracy). On BREC, the gains of EB-GNN cannot be attributed to triangle counting, as evidenced by the MPNN + C3 results. Remarkably, EB-GNN achieves performance on Basic and Regular graphs that is nearly identical to 22WL, though it fails to distinguish any CFI pairs. These results indicate that EB-GNN’s empirically realized expressivity extends well beyond triangle counting and, in many cases, approaches 22WL expressivity while maintaining significantly faster runtimes.

Molecular edge-level and graph-level tasks.

Table 1 presents the edge-level and graph-level results on QMD, compared against the baseline D-MPNN (Li et al., 2024). EB-GNN outperforms D-MPNN across all edge-level tasks, reducing the mean absolute error by 20% to 50% depending on the task. On graph-level tasks, EB-GNN and D-MPNN perform comparably, with EB-GNN slightly outperforming D-MPNN on two tasks and slightly underperforming on the other two. Table 4 summarizes the results on QM9, where we compare against several expressive GNNs. The current state-of-the-art on this dataset is 5-ℓ\ellGNN (Paolino et al., 2024), which significantly improved over previous architectures. EB-GNN ranks as the best or second-best model on 11 out of 12 tasks, achieving comparable or better performance than 5-ℓ\ellGNN on 7 tasks (with at most 6% lower accuracy) and outperforming it on 4 tasks. Moreover, EB-GNN is substantially more computationally efficient than 5-ℓ\ellGNN: while 5-ℓ\ellGNN has asymptotic runtime 𝒪⁡(n​d5)\mathcal{O}\left(nd^{5}\right), EB-GNN only requires 𝒪⁡(α​m)\mathcal{O}\left(\alpha m\right) time. In our experiments, EB-GNN is approximately 4 times faster (see App. A).

Results on graph-level tasks for malware detection.

Table 3 shows the results on MalNet-Tiny. EB-GNN outperforms all other models, including a standard MPNN, various graph transformers (GPS), and the subgraph GNN HyMN, demonstrating that EB-GNN generalizes well to other domains and scales effectively to larger graphs.

7 Conclusion, Limitations and Future Work

We propose an edge-based message passing algorithm that combines high expressivity with near-linear runtime on sparse graphs. Our analysis fully characterizes its expressivity in terms of first-order logic and establishes a meaningful lower bound via homomorphism counting. Empirically, our architecture outperforms standard MPNNs while remaining competitive with more expressive models, all at a substantially lower runtime. We observe that EB-GNN is a general-purpose architecture: while it achieves strong empirical results, it does not rely on specialized techniques used on top of basic architectures known to improve GNN performance, such as using subgraph counts (Bouritsas et al., 2022), homomorphism counts (Barceló et al., 2021; Welke et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2024) or positional encodings (You et al., 2019; Ying et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2023; Bao et al., 2025).

Limitations. Although EB-1WL and EB-GNN achieve near-linear running times for sparse graphs, their efficiency depends on arboricity and triangle enumeration, which can be expensive on very dense graphs, potentially limiting scalability in such settings. Furthermore, EB-GNN produces embeddings only for edges preventing direct application to node-level tasks and standard link-prediction methods that rely on node embeddings. We leave extending EB-GNN to these tasks as future work.

Future work. An interesting open problem left by our work is whether the converse of Thm. 3 holds, i.e., whether graphs distinguishable by EB-1WL are exactly those distinguishable by homomorphism counts from some chordal graph of treewidth 2. Another line of future work concerns the tradeoff between expressiveness and generalization: recent results show that greater expressiveness need not harm generalization if matched to task demands and training data (Maskey et al., 2025), and can even help when graphs are well separated by large margins (Li et al., 2025). EB-GNNs strike a principled balance — more expressive than NC-1WL, yet far cheaper than 2WL — while showing strong results across benchmarks. Future work should broaden empirical evaluation to fully assess this balance of expressiveness, scalability, and generalization.

Appendix A More Details on Experiments

We provide additional information on our experimental procedure and more detailed results.

Model.

We have defined graph as purely existing of nodes and edges G=(V,E)G=(V,E) . However, real-world datasets often use node features and edge features to encode additional information in the graph for all. For every directed edge (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E, we incorporate the node features of Xu,XvX_{u},X_{v} of u,vu,v and the edge features W(u,v)W_{(u,v)} of (u,v)(u,v) into our model by initializing the edge embedding 𝒯(0)​(G,(u,v)){\cal T}^{(0)}(G,(u,v)) with them. We use three different embedding encoders ENC to map both the node features and the edge features to the embedding dimension of our GNN

𝒯(0)​(G,(u,v))=ENCleft​(Xu)+ENCright​(Xv)+ENCedge​(W(u,v)).{\cal T}^{(0)}(G,(u,v))=\text{ENC}_{\text{left}}\left(X_{u}\right)+\text{ENC}_{\text{right}}\left(X_{v}\right)+\text{ENC}_{\text{edge}}\left(W_{(u,v)}\right).

After obtaining the initial edge embedding, we perform multiple iterations of edge based message passing. After final iteration tt, we pool edge embeddings into the shape required by the task. For graph-level tasks, we experiment with three methods. We compute graph-level embeddings by either summing

𝒯SUM(G)=∑(u,v):{u,v}∈E𝒯t(G,(u,v)),{\cal T}_{\text{SUM}}(G)=\sum\limits_{(u,v):\{u,v\}\in E}{\cal T}^{t}(G,(u,v)),

computing the mean, or computing the mean scaled by the number of nodes (mimicking sum pooling in MPNNs)

𝒯MEAN​(G)\displaystyle{\cal T}_{\text{MEAN}}(G) =1|E|​𝒯SUM​(G),\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{|E|}{\cal T}_{\text{SUM}}(G), 𝒯NODESUM​(G)\displaystyle\qquad{\cal T}_{\text{NODESUM}}(G) =|V||E|​𝒯SUM​(G).\displaystyle=\tfrac{|V|}{|E|}{\cal T}_{\text{SUM}}(G).

For edge-level tasks, note that we compute embeddings of directed edges whereas tasks we worked on were on undirected regression edges. we experiment with two methods of performing undirected edge predictions. First, we simply sum the embedding of the two directed edges and perform a prediction on this combined embedding. Second, we make a prediction for both directions and combine these predictions by computing the mean.

All our models were implemented in PyTorch Geometric (Paszke et al., 2019; Fey & Lenssen, 2019). All our models were trained on servers with one NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 GPU (10 GB VRAM) and 64 GB of RAM. When training a model we evaluate its performance after every epoch on the validation and test set. This performance is measured in the metric that is most commonly used on that dataset. After training, we report the validation and test performance in the epoch with the best validation performance. For real-life datasets, we perform hyperparameter tuning where we pick the hyperparameter combination based on the best validation performance. We train a model with this hyperparameter combination multiple times on different seeds reporting the mean and standard deviation of the test metric.

In general, all our models are trained with a Cosine learning rate scheduler and a learning rate of 0.0010.001 (except on BREC where we use the procedure provided by Wang & Zhang (2024)). The final prediction, is made by a two-layer MLP. On all real-life datasets EB-GNN uses both skip connections and feed-forward layers, but not on the synthetic datasets CSL and BREC. Below, we discuss the different setup we used for each dataset. For more details, please consider our code at https://github.com/ocatias/EdgeBasedGNNs.

CSL.

We train all models for 1000 epochs with a Cosine learning rate scheduler. All GNNs have 5 layers and an embedding dimension of 64.

BREC.

We train and evaluate our model with the procedure provided by Wang & Zhang (2024). Our EB-GNN model has 10 layers, an embedding dimension of 16 and uses some pooling. We have observed that using the output of Eq. 9 instead of Eq. 10 as edge embeddings leads to better results on the extension graphs. We believe that this is due to numerical issues caused by the large number of layers and small embedding dimension (which is necessary to fit the model into GPU memory). Our MPNN models also have 10 layers but uses an embedding dimension of 64.

QMD.

We train separate models for each of the 8 different tasks. We tune the hyperparameters of EB-GNN for each task based on the grid in Table 5. We train for 500 epochs with a batch size of 1024 and evaluate on 10 different seeds.

QM9.

We train separate models for each of the 11 different tasks. Initially, we repeated the same procedure as for QMD. However, training with a significantly larger batch size than models in literature might harm our performance. Thus, after the initial hyperparameter sweep (Table 5) we used the best hyperparameters and additionally tuned the batch size together with another pooling operation (Tab. 6). We evaluate the best hyperparameter combination on 10 different seeds.

Similar to Zhou et al. (2023) and Paolino et al. (2024), we perform a speed evaluation on QM9. For this, we train our model on the training set with batch size 64 and measure the time it takes to train for a single epoch. Additionally, we also track the pre-processing time on the entire dataset. The results can be seen in Tab. 7. There are two issues with this type of evaluation. First, we (as well as previous work) compare runtime of models trained on different hardware. This is best noticed by the fact that our expressive EB-GNN is faster than the MPNN in Tab. 7. In our case, this is less of a problem because compared to 5ℓ\ell-GIN (the other best model on QM9), our GPU is significantly weaker (RTX 3080 vs RTX 3090 Ti/RTX A6000). Second, we believe that previous works included the initial processing time for the dataset in pre-processing. This includes time spent to generate the initial graphs which is needed for all models but can vary across hardware. We remedy this by reporting both the time spent for our pre-processing (70 seconds) as well as the time spent on preparing the initial graphs (30 seconds).

MalNet-Tiny.

As the graphs in MalNet-Tiny are very large, we did not perform any hyperparameter tuning. Our model uses mean pooling, has 5 message passing layers and an embedding dimension of 64. It is trained for 500 epochs with a batch size of 16 and evaluated on 5 different seeds.
